To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the four existing approaches to mentoring preservice teachers during student teaching, while each has a distinct focus and set of practices, are not sufficient to guide the preservice teachers to meet the expectations of the field based teacher preparation reform.

(a) the four existing approaches to mentor teacher support of preservice teachers' student teaching experiences are grounded in different conceptual bases; (b) each approach focuses on a different dimension of preservice teacher learning to teach; (c) each approach involves different mentoring practices; and (d) each approach has its own challenges in guiding preservice teacher learning.

the field based teacher educator reforms have created new and unique functions for mentor teachers, and that the four existing approaches to mentoring preservice teachers during their student teaching are not sufficient to guide them to learn to teach to the extent expected by the reforms.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: How do teacher education faculty members conceptualize teacher mentoring during student-teaching? What are the characteristics and challenges of each approach to teacher mentoring? What can be learned from each approach to teacher education? What are the implications of the findings for the field-based teacher education reforms?
the question: What conceptual bases, characteristics, and challenges are associated with existing approaches to teacher mentorship during student teaching?
the question of how teacher mentoring can be conceptualized and practiced to best serve the learning needs of preservice teachers in the context of field based teacher education.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the field based teacher mentoring approaches to student teaching are not only necessary, but also effective, if properly implemented.
teacher mentoring is not only an important component of teacher education reform, but also a critical component that can help to determine the success or failure of the teacher education reform.

a teacher mentoring program should be conceptualized as a collaborative effort of all stakeholders to provide the preservice teachers with a comprehensive and well-planned program of teacher mentoring that includes a variety of mentoring activities to support preservice teacher learning at different levels of learning to teach.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

teacher mentoring in service of preservice teachers' field-based learning to teach is a complex and challenging process, which calls for the development of new conceptual frameworks and practices to guide preservice teachers to develop their knowledge and skills in the teaching profession.

teacher mentoring for preservice teacher education should be conceptualized as an integrated approach that focuses on both the preservice teachers' and mentor teachers' learning to improve teaching and learning.

teacher education reform calls for an integrated approach to mentoring preservice teachers that is based on a constructivist view of learning and teaching and that is informed by the research base on teacher learning and development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a more comprehensive and coherent approach to teacher mentoring is needed for the success of the field based teacher educator reforms.

a more integrated approach to teacher mentorship is needed to guide preservice teachers to develop the knowledge and dispositions for teaching as expected by the current field based teacher education reform.
the field based teacher preparation reforms call for a new approach to teacher mentoring, which is more holistic, comprehensive, and systematic in guiding preservice teacher learning to teach.
